drug_class: Anti-VEGF (vascular endothelial growth factor inhibitor) / Ophthalmic biologic agent
purpose: Brolucizumab is used to treat a serious eye condition called wet age-related macular degeneration (wet AMD), which can cause vision loss. It helps slow down or stop the growth of abnormal, leaky blood vessels in the back of your eye. This medication can help protect your vision and in some cases may even improve it.
how_it_works: In wet AMD, your body makes too much of a protein called VEGF, which causes abnormal blood vessels to grow and leak fluid under the retina — the light-sensitive area at the back of your eye. Brolucizumab works by blocking VEGF so those leaky vessels stop growing and the fluid dries up. Think of it like turning off a leaky faucet inside your eye to protect your sight.
common_side_effects: The most common side effects include blurry vision, eye pain or discomfort, a feeling of something in your eye, seeing floaters (small specks or lines in your vision), mild redness of the eye, and increased eye pressure. These are usually temporary, but let your doctor know if anything bothers you.
warnings: This medication is given as an injection directly into the eye, so there is a small risk of serious eye infection (endophthalmitis) or retinal detachment — seek urgent care if you have sudden vision changes, eye pain, or increased redness after your injection. Rarely, some patients have experienced inflammation inside the eye or blockage of blood vessels in the eye (including retinal artery or vein occlusion), which can cause serious vision problems. Tell your doctor about all your medications and health conditions before starting treatment, and always attend your follow-up eye appointments.
typical_dosing: Brolucizumab is given as an injection into your eye by your eye doctor (ophthalmologist) in a clinical setting — you will not give this to yourself at home. The typical schedule starts with one injection every 4 weeks for the first 3 doses (about 3 months), and then your doctor will evaluate your eyes and may switch you to an injection every 8 to 12 weeks depending on how your eyes are responding. Your doctor will personalize your schedule based on your individual needs.
